facts.statement: The Saint Helena rail was an extinct flightless rail native to the island of Saint Helena.
facts.quote: The Saint Helena rail (Aphanocrex podarces) is an extinct species of flightless rail from Saint Helena.

facts.statement: The species disappeared from Saint Helena in the early 16th century.
facts.quote: It disappeared from the island in the early 16th century.

facts.statement: In 1973, paleontologist Storrs Olson synonymized the genus Aphanocrex with the genus Atlantisia.
facts.quote: However, in 1973 American paleontologist Storrs Olson synonymised this genus with the genus Atlantisia, the other representative of which was the Inaccessible Island rail (Atlantisia rogersi).

facts.statement: It is debated whether the Saint Helena rail is closely related to the Inaccessible Island rail, leading some scientists to retain it in the genus Aphanocrex rather than Atlantisia.
facts.quote: While Olson had considered it as congener of the Inaccessible Island rail, other scientists regarded it not even as a close relative and so it is retained in Aphanocrex.

facts.statement: The Saint Helena rail was relatively large, reaching almost the size of the New Zealand weka.
facts.quote: The Saint Helena rail was relatively large and reached almost the size of the New Zealand weka (Gallirallus australis).

facts.statement: Unlike the New Zealand weka, the Saint Helena rail had a more slender build.
facts.quote: In contrast to the weka it was more slender.

facts.statement: The species possessed strong toes with long claws that allowed it to climb and flutter up steep valley walls.
facts.quote: Furthermore, it had strong toes with long claws, which gave that species a good ability to climb and flutter up the steep valley walls.

facts.statement: The rail likely fed on the eggs and juveniles of various Saint Helena bird species as well as snails.
facts.quote: It fed probably on the eggs and the juveniles of several Saint Helena terrestrial and pelagic bird species and on snails.

facts.statement: Paleontologist Storrs Olson suggested that the rail may have scavenged food dropped by visiting seabirds.
facts.quote: Storrs Olson suggested that Aphanocrex may have fed on food dropped by visiting seabirds.

facts.statement: The species became extinct after 1502 due to introduced alien predators such as cats and rats.
facts.quote: Like other ground-nesting birds such as the Saint Helena crake and the Saint Helena hoopoe it became a victim of alien predators like cats and rats which were brought to Saint Helena after 1502.

facts.statement: The species was described by American ornithologist Alexander Wetmore in 1963 from subfossil remains found in Prosperous Bay.
facts.quote: La especie fue descrita por el ornitólogo estadounidense Alexander Wetmore en 1963 a partir de restos subfósiles encontrados en la bahía Próspera.

facts.statement: Wetmore initially classified the species in the new genus Aphanocrex, but Storrs Olson later moved it to the genus Atlantisia in 1973.
facts.quote: Wetmore lo clasificó en el nuevo género Aphanocrex, pero en 1973 el paleontólogo estadounidense Storrs Olson consideró que la especie estaba relacionada con el rasconcillo de Tristán de Acuña y la trasladó al género Atlantisia.

facts.statement: Current belief that the two species evolved separately has led to the species being reclassified into the monotypic genus Aphanocrex.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, en la actualidad se cree que ambas especies evolucionaron de forma separada y no existe una relación estrecha entre ellas, por lo tanto, se ha vuelto a clasificar en el género monotípico Aphanocrex.

facts.statement: It was a relatively large bird, reaching a size similar to the New Zealand weka.
facts.quote: Era un pájaro relativamente grande, alcanzando un tamaño similar al rascón weka de Nueva Zelanda (Gallirallus australis).

facts.statement: In contrast to the weka, it was more slender.
facts.quote: En contraste con el weka era más delgado.

facts.statement: It had strong toes with long claws, giving it the ability to climb and flutter up steep valley walls.
facts.quote: Además, tenía dedos fuertes con largas garras, lo que le dio a esa especie una buena capacidad para trepar y revolotear por las empinadas paredes del valle.

facts.statement: It likely fed on the eggs and chicks of various terrestrial and pelagic bird species of Saint Helena, as well as snails.
facts.quote: Se alimentaba probablemente de huevos y polluelos de varias especies de aves terrestres y pelágicas de Santa Elena y de caracoles.

facts.statement: Like other ground-nesting species, it was a victim of introduced predators like cats and rats brought to the island after 1502.
facts.quote: Al igual que otras especies que anidaban en el suelo, como la polluela de Santa Elena (Porzana astrictocarpus) y la abubilla de Santa Elena (Upupa antaios), fueron víctimas de depredadores introducidos como gatos y ratas, llevados a Santa Elena después de 1502.

facts.statement: The genus lived from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene, approximately 0.129 to 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Late Pleistocene to Holocene (0.129 to 0 million years ago)

rejected.statement: American ornithologist Alexander Wetmore described the species in 1963 based on subfossil remains found at Prosperous Bay, Saint Helena.
rejected.quote: When American ornithologist Alexander Wetmore described this species from subfossil remains which were found at Prosperous Bay, Saint Helena, he classified it into the new genus Aphanocrex.

rejected.statement: Because Saint Helena was predator-free until the 16th century, the rail lost the ability to fly but retained better-developed wings than those of the New Zealand weka.
rejected.quote: Since Saint Helena was predator free until the sixteenth century, the rail had lost its ability to fly but its wings were better developed like the wings of the rails from Inaccessible Island and Ascension Island.

rejected.statement: Because Saint Helena was free of predators until the 16th century, the bird lost the ability to fly, but its wings were apparently better developed than those of the Ascension Island rail and the Tristan Island rail.
rejected.quote: El hecho de que Santa Elena estuviera libre de depredadores hasta el siglo , hizo que el calamón de Santa Elena perdiera su capacidad de volar, sin embargo, aparentemente sus alas estaban mejor desarrolladas que las del rascón de Ascensión y del rasconcillo de Tristán de Acuña.
